opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came out of frustration with what was already out there. Most long-context evals people were using, like needle-in-a-haystack, have a basic flaw: the "needle" is semantically different from the rest of the haystack. You hide some odd sentence about a pizza recipe inside a pile of essays, and the model can basically spot it because it sticks out. So you get these beautiful charts showing near-perfect recall at a million tokens, and they don't tell you whether the model can actually *use* that context.

So we built an eval that removes those shortcuts. It uses hashes, random, incompressible strings, so there's nothing semantic for the model to latch onto. You give it a big list of hash pairs and ask it to complete them, and you can make it harder by requiring multiple hops, following a chain of hashes through the context. That forces the model to really store and retrieve information across the whole window, and to do some reasoning over it, not just pattern-match on something weird.

Why open source it? A few reasons. We wanted people to trust our claims. If we say our model handles very long contexts well, you should be able to check that against a benchmark that can't be gamed with cheap tricks. And as a field, we needed better measuring sticks. If everyone keeps optimizing for evals that are already saturated or easy to shortcut, we fool ourselves about progress. Putting it out there felt like a small contribution to making long-context research more honest, and it helps everyone, including us, see where the real gaps are.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts million-token recall claims with testing whether a model can actually use long-context information, framing the evaluation as a measure beyond context-window size.

r002.rationale: It says others can check Magic’s claims against the benchmark, but does not clearly identify comparing other architectures’ performance with Magic’s as a reason for open-sourcing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started from frustration. When we were building our models at Magic, we needed a way to actually know whether a model was using its context window, and the evaluations that existed just didn't tell us that. Needle-in-a-haystack is the classic example. You take a long document, you drop in a sentence like "the magic number is 42," and you ask the model for the magic number. The problem is that the needle is semantically completely out of place. It sticks out. So the model doesn't really have to reason over the context, it just has to notice the weird sentence. And a lot of these tests end up implicitly rewarding exactly the thing you don't want, which is the model relying on its prior knowledge rather than on what's in front of it.

So we built HashHop. The idea is you use random hashes, which carry no semantic information whatsoever, so there's no shortcut. The model can't guess. And then you make it multi-hop, so it has to chain several lookups together, and you shuffle the order so it can't just rely on things being adjacent. It's a much harsher test, and it's much closer to what you need if you want a model to, say, hold an entire codebase in context and actually reason about it.

And once we had it, the question of whether to open source it was pretty easy. First, we wanted other people to stop fooling themselves. If a lab announces a million-token context window and the only evidence is a green needle-in-a-haystack chart, that's not telling anyone much. We'd rather the whole field have a harder yardstick. Second, we wanted credibility for our own claims. If we say our model does well on long context, people should be able to verify that with the same tool instead of taking our word for it. And third, it's not where our edge is. The eval isn't the secret. The hard part is building a model that passes it. So giving the eval away costs us very little and hopefully moves everyone a bit further toward honest measurement.

r001.rationale: It contrasts announcing a million-token context window with providing a harder evaluation that shows whether models use long context effectively.

r002.rationale: It says others can verify Magic’s claims with the same tool and that the field can use a harder yardstick, but does not identify comparing other architectures’ performance with Magic’s as a reason.

astra-6.text:
We wanted to make it easier for people to test what long-context models can actually do. There’s a difference between accepting a huge number of tokens and reliably using the information in them. If you’re looking at a large codebase, for example, you need the model to find the relevant information without knowing in advance where it is.

By open sourcing the evaluation, we let people inspect the methodology, run it on other models, and challenge our assumptions. We thought that was more useful than just publishing a score and asking people to trust it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes accepting a large token count from reliably using information across a long context, framing the evaluation as more than reporting context-window size.

r002.rationale: It says others can run the evaluation on other models, but does not state that this enables comparing their architectures’ performance with Magic’s.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted people to be able to scrutinize the evaluation and reproduce the results. Long context is easy to claim, but it’s harder to show that a model can actually use information across that context. Open sourcing the evaluation lets others test their own models and helps make the discussion more concrete.
